The rank seal

The wax seal, developed. It borrows its vocabulary from the stamps it counts — perforation beading and a sunburst are already stampArt.ts's own devices — so the medal is the same family of object as the thing it is a medal for, rather than a trophy imported from somewhere else.

⚠ Exclusivity is not brightness. A brighter seal is just a paler seal. Two things carry it instead: the ornament accumulates (nothing → beading → rays → laurel → faceted rim and double ring), and the material changes at platinum — bronze, silver and gold are wax, with a poured edge and a broad sheen; platinum is not. Its edge is crisp, its highlight is a hard cold sliver and its rim is cut into facets. It stops being the same substance.

⚠ No SVG filters. The cast shadow is an offset copy, the deboss is three passes, the sheen is a gradient — because feGaussianBlur is unreliable in react-native-svg on Android and this has to be drawable by the app.

The cross, filling the seal — count underneath

⚠⚠ Two structural changes, not a bigger glyph. The well is gone — a cross that fills the seal cannot sit inside a pressed well, because the well's edge would cut across its arms — so the face runs to the cord and the cross is struck straight onto it. And the count has left the medal, which frees the whole face and turns the button from a pill containing an icon and some text into an object with a caption.

⚠ The relief is facets, not a gradient. A raised cross is a set of planes: each arm is split along its spine and each half is shaded by which way it faces the light. That is what a struck cross actually does, and no amount of soft shading on a flat silhouette imitates it. Plus a raised keyline under the arms, and the inner cross engraved into them rather than laid on top — so it reads as one object instead of two stacked ones.

⚠ One consequence outside this file: on the map the passport button is a horizontal pill. A medal with the count underneath is a stacked control and a different shape, and D-015's 60 dp tap floor then applies to the medal alone, since a caption is not a tap target. Worth settling before this is promoted.

⚠ And the solid version — no inner cross, a boss at the crossing instead. The inner cross is the first thing to die when the medal shrinks, so this is the honest comparison.

At the real button — 64 dp, and D-015's floor at 44

⚠ The column that decides. Inset above, solid below.

On the green it will sit on

The ring — seven options

⚠ One variable at a time. The body, the lighting, the material and the centre are identical across this row — only the ring changes. A study that moves two things at once cannot tell you which one you liked, which is how round 5 had to be thrown away whole rather than partly.

Drawn on gold, because it carries ornament without the platinum facets competing, and again on bronze, because a ring that only works on the showy rank is not a ring.

The current one, as the control.
Interlocking ovals, alternating light and dark. Denser than cord and unmistakably made.
Engine-turned waves from banknotes and watch dials. Closed rings, so it can never read as spokes.
Two sprigs closing at the top. The most medal-like, and the least neutral.
⚠ Deliberately the closest to the rejected chip, so the difference can be seen: reeding sits on the outer edge, is far finer, and is cut across the rim rather than dotted on the face.
A plain channel between two lines. The quietest option, and the one that lets the metal do all the talking.
No ring at all. Worth seeing, because it is the only way to know how much the ring is contributing.

The centre — the cross

The Cruz de Cristo — the cross of the Order of Christ, painted on the sails of the caravels. For an app named after a ship's prow that is the same world, and it is national iconography rather than island geography, so it puts no Madeira fact into app/.

⚠⚠ But it binds the product to Portugal in a way nothing else here does. D-017 exists so this app could ship for another island by swapping content/. A Portuguese cross on the rank medal would have to be removed to do that; a cottage or an anchor would not. That is a real cost and it is the project lead's to accept — written down so the day somebody asks "why is there a cross in the chrome?", the answer exists. The symbol itself is centuries old and freely used; there is no rights question, only a positioning one.

⚠ Watch the inner cross at 64 and 44 dp. Two tones are what make it that cross, and the inner one is the first thing to vanish when a medal gets small — which is why the solid version is drawn beside it.

Same discipline: everything else frozen, including the cord ring. Gold, bronze, and the real 64 dp button.

⚠ The flared cross with a plain one inset — two tones, which is the whole of what makes it that cross rather than any cross. The inner one is lighter, so it reads on metal the way the white inner cross reads on the red.
One silhouette, no inset. ⚠ Simpler, and the one most likely to still be a cross at 44 dp — the inner cross is the first thing to disappear when a medal gets small.
Cut clean out of the metal with the dark of the well behind it. The most graphic, and the only version that does not need the metal for its contrast.
⚠ The most specific to this app of anything drawn so far: a caravel’s sail carrying the cross, for an app named after the prow of the same ship.
Mounted inside a raised ring, the way an order’s badge is. ⚠ Adds a second ring inside the cord — worth checking it does not fight it.
Unchanged, so the crosses have something to be judged against.
Kept from the last pass as the other strong silhouette.
Kept as the other nautical option, and the one that binds the app to no country at all.

Side by side — what changed

⚠ Top row is the edition you chose, untouched. Bottom row is the refinement. Judging a change against a description is how round 5 slipped through; judging it against the thing it replaced is harder to fool.

Nothing was added. Every difference is light or material: an occlusion ring where the well meets the face, a machined lip at the rim, a second tighter shadow for contact, a bounce arc on the unlit side, a deeper press for the mark — and a per-rank falloff, so platinum's face turns over like a mirror and bronze's like something matte. Same hues throughout.

On a light map

⚠ The map is the one surface whose brightness the user chooses (D-026) and this button floats on it. A medal that only works on a dark ground is one half the users never see properly.

On green — the ground it will actually sit on

Most of this island is laurel forest and terraces. A gold seal on a green map is the real test, not a seal on a neutral panel.

Greyscale — the ranks with the colour taken away

⚠ The real test of whether ornament is doing the work. If the ranks are only distinguishable by hue, then colour-blind users have one rank and everybody else has five.
